title: SSH Brute Force: Detection and Response
summary: Detecting, triaging and containing repeated SSH authentication failures.
content:
# SSH Brute Force: Detection and Response

## What it looks like
An SSH brute force attack is a high volume of failed authentication attempts against one or
more accounts over SSH, usually from a single source address or a small set of them. In logs
it appears as repeated sshd "Failed password" or "Invalid user" events, often several per
second, frequently targeting root, admin, oracle, postgres and other common accounts.

A related pattern is password spraying: one or two attempts against each of many accounts.
The per-account count never trips a lockout threshold, so the signal is the breadth of
accounts touched from one source rather than the depth of attempts against one account.

## Detection
Alert when a single source address produces more than 5 failed SSH authentications against
the same account within 5 minutes, or fails against more than 5 distinct accounts in any
window. Raise severity when the source is external, when the targeted account is privileged,
or when a success follows a run of failures from the same address - that combination often
means the attacker found a working credential.

Watch for a successful login from an address that has only ever failed before. Correlate the
source address against threat intelligence and against your own history: an address that has
never previously authenticated is more suspicious than a known office IP fat-fingering a
password.

## Triage questions
Was any attempt successful? Which accounts were targeted, and is any of them privileged or
service-owned? Is the source internal or external? Is the volume consistent with a
misconfigured client retrying, such as a stale cron job or a backup agent with an expired key?

## Containment
Block the source address at the perimeter firewall. Lock any account that was successfully
authenticated from the hostile source and force a credential reset. Terminate active sessions
originating from that address. If a service account was involved, rotate its key and check
where else that key is deployed.

## Hardening
Disable password authentication entirely and require public keys. Disable direct root login.
Move SSH off the public internet behind a VPN or bastion host. Deploy fail2ban or an
equivalent to rate-limit repeated failures. Require MFA for bastion access. Ensure SSH
authentication logs are shipped centrally so an attacker with host access cannot erase them.
